title: Merge two sorted linked lists into one single sorted linked list. Both input lists are sorted in ascending order and you must return one combined list that is still sorted.
shortTitle: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists Into One Sorted List

s1_definition.profdef: Merging two sorted linked lists is the technique of combining two already-sorted singly linked lists into one sorted list by repeatedly comparing the head nodes of both lists and splicing the smaller node into the result. It runs in O(n plus m) time and O(1) extra space when done iteratively, because we only relink existing nodes rather than creating new ones.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) each hand the bank teller a pile of cheques already sorted by amount, smallest on top. The teller wants one single sorted pile. He looks at the top cheque of each pile, takes whichever amount is smaller, places it on the new pile, and repeats. When one pile is empty, he drops the rest of the other pile on top because it is already sorted. That is exactly how we merge two sorted linked lists.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a dummy head, always attach the smaller of the two current nodes, then attach whatever remains.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merging two sorted linked lists is the technique of combining two already-sorted singly linked lists into one sorted list by repeatedly comparing the head nodes of both lists and splicing the smaller node into the result. It runs in O(n plus m) time and O(1) extra space when done iteratively, because we only relink existing nodes rather than creating new ones.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) each hand the bank teller a pile of cheques already sorted by amount, smallest on top. The teller wants one single sorted pile. He looks at the top cheque of each pile, takes whichever amount is smaller, places it on the new pile, and repeats. When one pile is empty, he drops the rest of the other pile on top because it is already sorted. That is exactly how we merge two sorted linked lists.

**One line to remember:** Keep a dummy head, always attach the smaller of the two current nodes, then attach whatever remains.

sections.s2_technical:
A singly linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a reference to the next node. When two such chains are both sorted ascending, we can merge them without re-sorting because the smallest unused element is always at the head of one of the two lists.

The core trick is the dummy head node. We create one throwaway node called `dummy` and a moving pointer called `tail` that starts at `dummy`. For example, `ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0); ListNode tail = dummy;`. On each step we compare `a.val` and `b.val`. If `a.val <= b.val` we do `tail.next = a; a = a.next;` otherwise `tail.next = b; b = b.next;`. Then we advance `tail = tail.next;`. This is the splice operation, and it reuses the original nodes instead of allocating new ones.

When one list runs out, we attach the remainder in one move: `tail.next = (a != null) ? a : b;`. Because the leftover list is already sorted and all its values are at least as large as everything placed so far, we never need to inspect it node by node.

The result starts at `dummy.next`, never at `dummy` itself, because `dummy` was only a convenient anchor so that we did not have to special-case the first node.

A senior-level nuance is stability and the equal-value tie-break. Using `a.val <= b.val` (less-than-or-equal) keeps nodes from the first list before equal nodes from the second list, which preserves original order among equal keys. In banking, if two transactions have the identical amount, keeping the earlier-submitted one first can matter for audit ordering.

The recursive version is elegant but uses O(n plus m) stack frames, which risks a StackOverflowError on very long lists such as a full day of transaction records, so production code prefers the iterative loop.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs two settlement feeds every night. One feed carries Rajesh's savings-account debit instructions already sorted by amount, and another feed carries Priya's current-account debit instructions also sorted by amount. The settlement engine needs a single sorted stream of instructions so the ledger is written in one clean ascending pass. This is exactly how merging two sorted linked lists works — each feed is a sorted list, and we weave them into one sorted list.

Problem 2 — The engine must not re-sort, because each feed can hold millions of instructions and re-sorting would waste CPU during the narrow settlement window. This is why we exploit the fact that both lists are already sorted and simply compare heads. The merge is linear, not n-log-n.

Problem 3 — Money values must be exact, so each node carries a BigDecimal amount, never a double. We compare amounts using `compareTo`.

In the code: a `SettlementNode` class holds a transaction id, a BigDecimal amount, and a next pointer. A `SettlementMerger` class has a `merge` method that takes two sorted node chains and returns one. A `SettlementDemo` main method builds Rajesh's feed and Priya's feed, merges them, and logs the single sorted output.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh's feed is 1000, 5000, 9000. Priya's feed is 2000, 5000, 12000.

Step 1: We create a dummy node and a tail pointer sitting on dummy. Compare 1000 (Rajesh) and 2000 (Priya). 1000 is smaller, so we attach Rajesh's 1000 and advance Rajesh's pointer to 5000. Tail moves to 1000.

Step 2: Compare 5000 (Rajesh) and 2000 (Priya). 2000 is smaller, so we attach Priya's 2000 and advance Priya's pointer to 5000. Tail moves to 2000.

Step 3: Compare 5000 (Rajesh) and 5000 (Priya). They are equal, and because we use less-than-or-equal we take Rajesh's 5000 first for stable order. Advance Rajesh to 9000. Tail moves to 5000.

Step 4: Compare 9000 (Rajesh) and 5000 (Priya). 5000 is smaller, attach Priya's 5000. Advance Priya to 12000. Tail moves to 5000.

Step 5: Compare 9000 (Rajesh) and 12000 (Priya). 9000 is smaller, attach it. Rajesh's list is now empty.

Step 6: One list is empty, so we attach the remainder of Priya's list, which is just 12000. The merge is done.

```
         Priya  feed [2000 -> 5000 -> 12000]

  dummy -> tail
    │ compare heads 1000 vs 2000  → take 1000 (Rajesh)
    │ compare heads 5000 vs 2000  → take 2000 (Priya)
    │ compare heads 5000 vs 5000  → take 5000 (Rajesh, stable <=)
    │ compare heads 9000 vs 5000  → take 5000 (Priya)
    │ compare heads 9000 vs 12000 → take 9000 (Rajesh)
    │ Rajesh empty → attach remainder [12000]
    ▼
  Output: 1000 -> 2000 -> 5000(R) -> 5000(P) -> 9000 -> 12000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging two sorted linked lists is a classic linear-time, constant-space technique where you walk both lists at the same time and always attach the smaller of the two current head nodes to a result list that you grow from a dummy sentinel head. Because both inputs are already sorted, you never re-sort anything, so the whole operation is O(n plus m) rather than O(n log n).

The dummy head is the key trick. By starting the result with a throwaway node and a tail pointer, you avoid writing special-case code for the very first node, and you simply return dummy-dot-next at the end. When one list runs dry, you attach the entire remaining list in a single step because it is already sorted and its values are all at least as large as everything merged so far.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to combine two nightly settlement feeds, one from Rajesh's savings account and one from Priya's current account, both pre-sorted by amount, into a single ascending stream that the ledger writer consumes in one clean pass. I kept the amounts in BigDecimal and compared them with compareTo to stay exact, and I used less-than-or-equal on the tie so that equal amounts preserve their original feed order for audit stability.

I always use the iterative version in production rather than the recursive one, because a recursive merge consumes a stack frame per node and a full day of transactions could trigger a StackOverflowError. The iterative loop is just as short and completely safe on arbitrarily long lists.
